lesson.title: Spontaneous Recovery: The Response That Won't Quite Stay Gone
lesson.summary: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a weakened conditioned response after a rest period following extinction, even though the conditioned stimulus has not been paired with the unconditioned stimulus again.
lesson.body:
After a conditioned response has been extinguished, it can look like the learning is gone for good. But if the organism is given a break from the extinction procedure and the conditioned stimulus is presented again later, the conditioned response often reappears, at least briefly and usually in a weaker form than the original. This reappearance, without any new pairings of the conditioned stimulus and the unconditioned stimulus, is spontaneous recovery.

Pavlov noticed this in his own dogs. After extinguishing the salivation response by repeatedly presenting the tone with no food, he let some time pass and then presented the tone again. The dogs salivated again, even though the tone had never once been followed by food during that rest period. The recovered response was smaller than the original conditioned response, and if he kept presenting the tone alone, it extinguished again, typically faster than the first time.

Spontaneous recovery is good evidence for the point raised in the discussion of extinction: extinguishing a response suppresses it rather than deleting it outright. The original stimulus and response are still connected somewhere in the organism's learning history, just held in check by the newer, competing extinction learning. That is also part of why relapse is such a common feature of behaviors people are trying to unlearn, a food craving, a fear, a habit: the old association has not vanished, it has just gone quiet, and it can resurface under the right conditions, particularly after time has passed.
